stories.title: Javits Center Expansion, Tech Upgrades Boosting NYC Hospitality Industry
stories.excerpt: Five years after the Javits Center underwent a $1.5 billion expansion, the Hudson Yards convention venue is continuing to expand its bandwidth to boost its events business and the adjacent New York City hospitality industry. The 3.3 million-square-foot facility recently underwent a $5 million technology upgrade enabling the Javits Center to become the first convention center in the U.S. to provide the newest wireless network, Wi-Fi 7, Commercial Observer can first report. The Wi-Fi 7 system, which debuted last month for Fanatics Fest, provides another competitive edge in attracting more conferences and events going forward, Joyce Leveston, CEO of the Javits Center, told CO. “So many people who are coming to conventions also want to feel that they can remotely connect with their workplace,” Leveston said on Wednesday, moments before the Javits Center marked its 40th anniversary with a celebration event. “You can’t do that unless you have a state-of-the-art Wi-Fi system.” The technology enhancement is just the latest effort by the Javits Center to up the ante in terms of drawing some of the biggest conferences and events to Manhattan and providing a jolt to New York City’s economy. The Javits Center estimates that its convention bookings generated more than 100,000 hotel stays in the New York City region in 2025. The expansion of the Javits Center, which debuted in May 2021, added 1.2 million square feet to the north side of the complex, including a 55,000-square-foot ballroom and a glass-enclosed sustainable rooftop pavilion touted as the largest green roof in the Northeast. The boost to New York City’s hospitality industry from new investments to the Javits Center is evident across the street at 418 11th Avenue, where a new 455-room Hilton-branded hotel is slated to open in the next three years as part of a larger mixed-use project. bullets: Javits Center invests $5M in Wi-Fi 7 upgrade, first U.S. convention center.
Infrastructure improvement designed to attract larger conferences and multi-day events.
Hudson Yards venue expansion continues to drive NYC hospitality sector competition.
stories.summary: The Javits Center in Hudson Yards has completed a $5 million technology upgrade to deploy Wi-Fi 7 wireless connectivity, positioning itself as the first U.S. convention center with the latest network standard. The move is part of a broader push to attract major conferences and events. CEO Joyce Leveston emphasized the upgrade's role in allowing attendees to maintain remote workplace connectivity, a key competitive advantage for convention venues.
stories.impact: Modest indirect demand signal for Manhattan residential: large conference expansions drive temporary lodging demand and corporate travel, which can translate to short-term rental pressure and hotel-adjacent multifamily demand. However, this is incremental to existing Hudson Yards multifamily pipeline and unlikely to shift major acquisition/development strategy in NYC.

stories.title: River School Buys Tenleytown’s Under Oak Estate, Plans New Campus
stories.excerpt: The River School, a private school based in Washington, D.C., has purchased Under Oak, a two-lot estate in Tenleytown, with plans to build a new campus on the 2.27-acre property. Located at 4220 Nebraska Ave. NW, a block south of American University’s Tenleytown campus, the property sold for $8.75 million, reported the Washington Business Journal. Known for its gardens and a 400-year-old oak tree that once stood on the site, the property has been under contract with The River School for six years. The River School, with a main campus at 4880 MacArthur Blvd. NW, closed on the property after the D.C. Court of Appeals dismissed a challenge to the institution’s plans filed by the Tenleytown Preservation Association. The Tenleytown estate has belonged to Ruth Hale Buchanan, the late socialite, philanthropist and granddaughter of Dow Chemical Co.’s founder. Sassy Jacobs and Ben Roth of Washington Fine Properties represented the Buchanan estate as seller. JM Zell Partners represented The River School throughout the entitlement and sale processes. The post River School Buys Tenleytown’s Under Oak Estate, Plans New Campus appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: River School acquires 2.27-acre Tenleytown estate for $8.75M, builds new campus.
Six-year entitlement fight resolved; D.C. Court of Appeals dismissed preservation challenge.
Educational institution expansion removes residential/mixed-use development opportunity from Washington market.
stories.summary: The River School, a private Washington D.C.-based institution, has purchased the Under Oak estate at 4220 Nebraska Ave. NW in Tenleytown for $8.75 million after a six-year entitlement battle. The D.C. Court of Appeals dismissed a challenge from the Tenleytown Preservation Association, clearing the way for the school to build a new campus on the historic 2.27-acre property. The estate was previously owned by the Buchanan family (granddaughter of Dow Chemical founder).
stories.impact: Negative supply signal for Washington D.C. multifamily, particularly Upper Northwest submarkets: loss of a prime infill development site (2.27 acres in walkable, established Tenleytown) to institutional use removes a potential residential acquisition target. Educational expansion is unlikely to generate rental demand sufficient to offset lost development opportunity—signals continued pressure on land availability in established D.C. neighborhoods.

stories.title: Manhattan Apartment Rents Reach Record High Amid Declining Inventory
stories.excerpt: Average Manhattan apartment rents reached an all-time high of $6,655 in July, according to Corcoran Sunshine Marketing Group. Median rents held steady at June’s record-setting level of $5,295, up 6% from a year ago. “Meanwhile, the number of signed leases rose 3% annually, while inventory dropped a substantial 22% over the same period,” said Corcoran Group COO Gary Malin. “This increased demand for apartments in the borough, coupled with reduced supply, has created a pressure cooker. Too many would-be tenants are seeking a shrinking number of available apartments. The city desperately needs to unlock or build more rental housing.” Corcoran Sunshine reported more moderate conditions in Brooklyn, where the median rent declined slightly month-over-month to $4,257. Even so, Brooklyn inventory declined year-over-year while lease signings rose, as in Manhattan. “New York’s unmatched appeal continues to attract people looking to put down roots, but years of policies that have discouraged investment by owners and developers have helped push rents and competition to new extremes,” Malin said. The post Manhattan Apartment Rents Reach Record High Amid Declining Inventory appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Manhattan rents hit record $6,655 average; median rent $5,295, up 6% YoY.
Inventory plunged 22% YoY while signed leases rose 3% annually.
Brooklyn median rents declined to $4,257 despite inventory drop and rising lease signings.
stories.summary: Manhattan apartment rents reached an all-time high of $6,655 average in July, with median rents steady at $5,295 (up 6% year-over-year), according to Corcoran Sunshine Marketing Group. Inventory dropped a substantial 22% year-over-year while signed leases rose 3%, creating acute supply-demand imbalance. Brooklyn showed more moderation with median rents at $4,257, though it too experienced inventory decline and rising lease activity. Corcoran COO Gary Malin warned the city "desperately needs to unlock or build more rental housing."
stories.impact: Critical development signal for Manhattan and outer-borough multifamily: extreme rent growth (+6% YoY) coupled with 22% inventory collapse indicates severe undersupply and strong pricing power, creating high-yield development environment. However, note the implicit warning: regulatory/policy headwinds are discouraging new supply, meaning acquisition and entitlement velocity matter more than ever. Outer-borough plays (Brooklyn, Queens) likely offer better risk-adjusted returns than Manhattan given regulatory uncertainty; consider land banking in transit-adjacent Queens submarkets ahead of zoning relief.

stories.title: JLL Secures $40M Refinancing for Multifamily in Portland’s Lloyd District
stories.excerpt: JLL has secured a $40.5 million refinancing for The Payton, a 162-unit multifamily property in Portland, Oregon. JLL represented the borrower, ColRich, in arranging the five-year, floating-rate loan through Prime Finance. The Payton, located at 2020 NE Multnomah St., is a seven-story mid-rise community built in 2019. JLL Capital Market’s Debt Advisory team was led by Senior Managing Director Aldon Cole, Managing Director Jimmy Conley, Directors Brock Knapp and Sean O’Brien, and Analysts Ben Choromanski and Matthew Payamps. The property sits at the confluence of Portland’s Central Eastside and Lloyd District, two of the metro area’s most centrally located urban submarkets, with over five million square feet of retail within one mile. The property maintains 98% occupancy as of August 2026. “The successful refinancing of The Payton demonstrates the positive momentum in Portland’s multifamily market and the quality of ColRich’s long-term ownership strategy,” said Cole. bullets: JLL secures $40.5M five-year floating-rate refi for 162-unit Portland property.
The Payton (2019, 98% occupied) refinances at Lloyd District/Central Eastside confluence.

stories.summary: JLL arranged a $40.5 million five-year floating-rate refinancing for The Payton, a 162-unit mid-rise multifamily property in Portland's Lloyd District (2020 NE Multnomah St.), built in 2019. The refinancing was arranged through Prime Finance for borrower ColRich. The property maintains 98% occupancy and benefits from its proximity to over five million square feet of retail within one mile, positioning it in Portland's most centrally located urban submarket.
stories.impact: Moderately positive signal for Portland development: successful refi of newer mid-rise asset at 98% occupancy with floating-rate debt suggests lender confidence in Lloyd District/Central Eastside fundamentals and rental resilience. Strong occupancy and capital availability indicate the submarket has stabilized post-pandemic downturn. For development teams, this signals a window to underwrite new mid-rise projects in central Portland with conviction on rent growth and occupancy, though floating-rate risk requires careful pro-forma stress-testing.

stories.title: Cushman & Wakefield Arranges $37M Financing for MD Mixed-Used Development
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield has arranged $37.37 million in floating-rate construction financing for Derby Place, a 94,587-square-foot retail development anchored by Whole Foods Market in Bel Air, Maryland. The property is already 92% committed with retailers and service providers. Located at 610 Baltimore Pike, Derby Place will feature 60,000 square feet of luxury boutiques, restaurants, shops and amenities. The development will offer 512 parking spaces on a 10.45-acre site. Derby Place will replace a vacant Macy’s location at the former Harford Mall. Cushman & Wakefield’s Equity, Debt & Structured Finance team of John Alascio, Mark Gilbert, Alex Hernandez, and Mitch Rothstein represented the borrower, SJC Ventures, in securing the financing. SJC Ventures recently began the demolition process of the former Macy’s. Bank of America provided the loan. “This transaction exemplifies the continued demand for institutional-quality, grocery-anchored retail in high-barrier markets,” said Gilbert. bullets: C&W arranges $37.37M floating-rate construction financing for Derby Place, Bel Air, MD.
Grocery-anchored retail (Whole Foods) with 60K SF luxury tenant mix, 92% committed.
Replaces vacant Macy's at former Harford Mall on 10.45-acre parcel.
stories.summary: Cushman & Wakefield arranged $37.37 million in floating-rate construction financing for Derby Place, a 94,587-square-foot retail development in Bel Air, Maryland, anchored by Whole Foods Market. The property is already 92% committed with retailers and service providers, offering 60,000 square feet of luxury boutiques, restaurants, and shops on a 10.45-acre site with 512 parking spaces. Bank of America provided the loan; SJC Ventures is the borrower.
stories.impact: Tangential to multifamily; primarily retail/mixed-use signal. However, notes Bel Air as a high-barrier suburban Maryland market attracting institutional capital for experiential retail (Whole Foods + luxury amenities), suggesting demographic strength in Baltimore metro suburbs. Indirect upside: retail-anchored development success in Bel Air could signal ancillary demand for transit-adjacent rental housing in secondary Baltimore submarkets, but this is speculative. Not a primary multifamily development catalyst.

stories.title: Fortress Refinances Dania Design Center With $45M After Foreclosure Fight
stories.excerpt: Fortress Investment Group has refinanced the Design Center of the Americas in Dania Beach, Fla., following a nasty foreclosure fight with its previous owner, New York-based billionaire Charles Cohen. City National Bank of Florida supplied a $45 million loan backing the 780,000-square-foot office and design showroom complex at 1855 Griffin Road, facing the I-95. In the past two years, Fortress has invested about $3 million updating the campus, which dates back to 1988. Another $3 million to $5 million of renovations are planned over the coming year. In June, it tapped Jamestown to oversee management and leasing of the mixed-use property. The move comes about five years after the Design Center lost one of its main tenants, online pet retailer Chewy, which occupied about 100,000 square feet, when it relocated to Plantation Pointe. Fortress won control of Design Center and the neighboring Le Méridien Dania Beach hotel in 2024, through a $76 million credit bid. The proceeding was part of a broader foreclosure suit with Cohen Realty Enterprises, which Charles Cohen’s father Sherman Cohen had founded in the 1950s. In 2022, the New York-based lender provided a $535 million debt package, covering several commercial properties, including Cohens’s Dania Beach assets. The billionaire also personally guaranteed a $187 million portion of the loan. A year later, Cohen defaulted, prompting Fortress to take control of the commercial real estate. The lender also went after the borrower’s personal assets, believing the commercial properties were worth less than what Cohen owed, the Wall Street Journal reported. These include a chateau and vineyard estate in the south of France, a 220-foot megayacht, and a collection of Ferraris. In response, Cohen sold off several properties in New York. In June, Cohen announced that he had paid off the full judgement. But the legal battle remains, with Cohen filing to recoup $204 million in alleged damages. bullets: Fortress refinances Design Center of the Americas (Dania, FL) with $45M City National loan.

stories.summary: Fortress Investment Group has refinanced the Design Center of the Americas in Dania Beach, Florida, a 780,000-square-foot office and design showroom complex, with a $45 million loan from City National Bank of Florida. Fortress acquired the property via a $76 million credit bid in 2024 following a foreclosure fight with billionaire Charles Cohen. The firm has invested approximately $3 million in upgrades and plans an additional $3–5 million in renovations over the coming year; it engaged Jamestown as property manager and leasing agent in June.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance; primarily distressed office/mixed-use repositioning in South Florida. However, signals that Fortress (large institutional investor) is actively capital-cycling distressed assets in Dania/Broward and pivoting to professional management, suggesting selective institutional appetite for South Florida deals near completion. Indirectly, successful stabilization of large office/mixed-use projects in I-95 corridor could drive ancillary multifamily demand (workforce housing near employment centers), but unlikely to shift major development priorities absent residential conversion signals.

stories.title: MDH Partners Acquires 1M-SF Industrial Building in Indiana
stories.excerpt: MDH Partners (MDH) has acquired 70 Connect III, a 1,005,776-square-foot industrial building in Greenfield, Indiana, part of the Indianapolis metropolitan area. The building, developed by Lauth, was delivered on a speculative basis and sits along West 350 North in the East industrial submarket. JLL represented the seller in the transaction. MDH’s Director of Acquisitions, Houston Hawley, led the acquisition for the firm. JLL’s Brian Buschuk and Brian Seitz will handle leasing for MDH. “We’re ultimately believers in quality assets at a good basis, and that’s exactly what we’re getting with 70 Connect III,” Hawley said. The cross-docked building offers 40-foot clear heights, 108 dock doors expandable to 216, four drive-in doors, an ESFR sprinkler system and eight-inch slabs. The site has two points of entry along West 350 North and is less than three miles from Interstate 70 and about ten miles from Interstate 465, Indianapolis’ primary loop. The Indianapolis International Airport and its FedEx hub are within a 30-mile drive. stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development. Indirect signal: sustained industrial demand near Indianapolis airports suggests continued wage employment growth in logistics/supply-chain sectors, which underpins broad rental demand in Indianapolis metro. Monitor for parallel multifamily acquisitions in secondary Indianapolis submarkets (Greenfield, Plainfield, Avon) proximate to industrial job centers.

stories.title: Keystone Equities Provides $61M Acquisition Debt for IOS Repositioning Site in Newark
stories.excerpt: KS Group has secured $60.5 million in acquisition debt to buy a 51-acre industrial site in Newark, N.J., that will be repositioned as an industrial outdoor storage property, Commercial Observer can first report. Keystone Equities provided the debt, structured as a senior bridge loan, marking $660 million in capital the firm has deployed since August 2023, the firm noted in a release. KS Group is buying the site from an ownership group led by Daryl Hagler. CBRE’s Shlomo Weissberg and Eli Klapper arranged the transaction. Jonathan Zamir, founder and CEO of Keystone Equities, noted in a statement that the site is currently under active environmental remediation and still hadn’t secured a certificate of occupancy before closing, which led to several “traditional lenders” to decline to underwrite the risk associated with the deal. “This was a deal that required real diligence. We dug in, structured around the risks, and found a solution that works for both us and the borrower,” he said. “That’s where Keystone adds value.” Located at 151 Raymond Boulevard in Newark, the industrial site is a former PSEG property that holds proximity to Port Newark-Elizabeth and New York City. The new IOS site will include parking for both trucks and trailers, a container garage for shipping, and electric vehicle and solar charging stations. CBRE noted in recent reports that IOS vacancy in Northern New Jersey stands at 2.5 percent, while rents have grown 123 percent since 2020. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Keystone Equities provides $60.5M senior bridge loan for 51-acre Newark industrial site.
KS Group repositioning site as outdoor storage; under environmental remediation, no COO at close.
Bridge financing deployed because traditional lenders declined environmental/remediation risk.
stories.summary: KS Group has secured $60.5 million in acquisition debt from Keystone Equities to purchase a 51-acre industrial site in Newark, New Jersey (151 Raymond Boulevard) that will be repositioned as an industrial outdoor storage property. The deal was structured as a senior bridge loan because the site is undergoing active environmental remediation and lacked a certificate of occupancy at closing, causing traditional lenders to decline underwriting the risk. Keystone Equities has deployed $660 million in capital since August 2023.
stories.impact: Negative signal for Newark residential/mixed-use development: large industrial-suitable parcel (51 acres) in central Newark market will be converted to outdoor storage, removing potential mixed-use redevelopment opportunity. However, bridge financing success signals that alternative lenders remain active in Northeast industrial repositioning, which may unlock other contaminated-site deals. For multifamily developers, this underscores the competitive challenge of acquiring infill sites in legacy industrial markets—environmental remediation timelines and lender conservatism create extended holding periods, favoring pure-play industrial operators over residential developers.

stories.title: Zimmet Law Group Relocates to 5K SF at GFP’s 515 Madison Avenue
stories.excerpt: Zimmet Law Group is relocating its practice inside Manhattan’s Plaza District. Zimmet signed a 5,476-square-foot lease for a newly completed space inside GFP Real Estate’s 515 Madison Avenue, also known as the DuMont Building. Located at the corner of East 53rd Street, the 42-story office tower is just one block south of Zimmet’s current abode in RFR Holding’s 477 Madison Avenue. Zimmet’s practice areas range widely, from matrimonial and family law to real estate matters. The law firm was represented by Savitt Partners’ Elliot Zelinger, while GFP’s Martin McGrath and Kephra Stone negotiated in-house for the landlord. Zelinger did not respond to a request for comment. Asking rent for the nearly 10-year lease term was not disclosed, but office asking rents in Midtown averaged $88.50 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to Cushman & Wakefield data. Zimmet is expected to take occupancy at 515 Madison later this year, according to GFP, following the completion of its new space. Zimmet’s office did not respond to a request for comment on the relocation. Earlier this year, GFP took full ownership of the 350,000-square-foot Class A tower after securing an $86.5 million refinancing deal with Apple Bank, which enabled the buyout of ATCO Properties & Management’s remaining 40 percent stake in the property. By late February, the landlord had secured 12,000 square feet of new leasing activity, Commercial Observer reported. GFP announced another 9,000 square feet of deals in late July, including leases for investment firm T7 Capital, aesthetic training provider Innovation Training Specialist and Widowski Law Group. Other tenants at 515 Madison include alternative asset manager Whitebox and therapy provider Manhattan Psychiatry Group. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Zimmet Law Group leases 5,476 SF at GFP's 515 Madison Avenue (DuMont Building).
Tenant relocating within Plaza District; midtown Manhattan office rents averaged $88.50/SF in Q2 2026.
GFP completed new space; occupancy expected late 2026.
stories.summary: Zimmet Law Group has signed a lease for a newly completed 5,476-square-foot space at 515 Madison Avenue (the DuMont Building), located at the corner of East 53rd Street in Midtown Manhattan. The firm is relocating from 477 Madison Avenue (one block north) within the Plaza District. Asking rents for the nearly 10-year lease term were not disclosed, but Midtown Manhattan office asking rents averaged $88.50 per square foot in Q2 2026, according to Cushman & Wakefield data.
stories.impact: Not relevant to multifamily development. Signals only modest Plaza District office leasing activity and continued premium rents in Midtown—neither of which affects residential acquisition/development strategy. Office market stability in Midtown is backdrop noise for multifamily teams focused on Manhattan rental fundamentals.

stories.title: Sixth Street Acquires Iconic Pier House Hotel in Key West for $190M
stories.excerpt: An iconic luxury hotel in Key West, Fla., is changing hands. Sixth Street Partners and Riller Capital have acquired Pier House, a longstanding 142-room oceanfront resort in downtown Key West, from Braemar Hotels & Resorts in a $190 million deal, according to a release from Sixth Street. Starwood Property Trust provided the debt financing, the amount of which has not been disclosed, while the Plasencia Group advised Braemar Hotels & Resorts on the sale. Aman Gupta, principal at Sixth Street, noted in a statement that Pier House has access to a private beach and includes unobstructed sunset views for its guests while also being in the heart of Downtown Key West. “This investment reflects Sixth Street’s commitment to identifying high-quality hospitality assets where we can drive long-term value,” said Gupta. Located at 1 Duval Street, Pier Street sits on five acres of beachfront land along the famous Duval Street, a top tourist destination and walkable retail and entertainment thoroughfare. The resort first opened in 1967 and had been owned by Braemar Hotels & Resorts since 2014. On-site amenities include two oceanfront restaurants, a spa, a fitness center, an oceanfront pool and 3,000 square feet of event space. “We believe Pier House represents an opportunity to acquire a historic luxury resort in one of the country’s most supply-constrained and sought-after tropical leisure markets,” said Gupta. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Sixth Street Partners acquires Pier House Resort (142 rooms) in Key West for $190M.
Oceanfront property on 5 acres; Starwood Property Trust provided debt.
Iconic beachfront asset on Duval Street; long-term value-add play for hospitality investor.
stories.summary: Sixth Street Partners and Riller Capital have acquired Pier House, a 142-room oceanfront resort in Key West, Florida, from Braemar Hotels & Resorts for $190 million. The luxury resort sits on five acres of beachfront property at 1 Duval Street, one of Key West's premier tourist and retail destinations. Starwood Property Trust provided debt financing. Sixth Street emphasized the acquisition reflects its strategy of identifying high-quality hospitality assets for long-term value creation.
stories.impact: Not relevant to multifamily development. Pure hospitality acquisition in destination leisure market (Key West). No residential demand signal or development opportunity; institutional capital flowing to asset classes unrelated to rental housing. No secondary-order multifamily effect.
